entries.3bcbd689f9ea106bc7f63adcbab12a2638c80c97: <div sID="gen16278" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="38" osisID="Isa.38" sID="Isa.38"/> <div eID="gen16278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16279" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16280" type="x-p"/> This chapter proceeds in the history of Hezekiah. Here is, I. His sickness, and the sentence of death he received within himself, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. His prayer in his sickness, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.2-Isa.38.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>. III. The answer of peace which God gave to that prayer, assuring him that he should recover, that he should live fifteen years yet, that Jerusalem should be delivered from the king of Assyria, and that, for a sign to confirm his faith herein, the sun should go back ten degrees, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.4-Isa.38.8">ver. 4-8</reference>. And this we read and opened before, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.1">2 Kings xx. 1</reference>, &c. But, IV. Here is Hezekiah's thanksgiving for his recovery, which we had not before, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.9-Isa.38.20">ver. 9-20</reference>. To which are added the means used (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.21">ver. 21</reference>), and the end the good man aimed at in desiring to recover, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.22">ver. 22</reference>. This is a chapter which will entertain the thoughts, direct the devotions, and encourage the faith and hopes of those that are confined by bodily distempers; it visits those that are visited with sickness.
entries.efa5ca1dc4f6e9153028bd1b275f197bd6e09baf: <div eID="gen16280" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16279" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Hezekiah's Sickness. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen16281" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> In those days was Hezekiah sick unto death. And Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz came unto him, and said unto him, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Set thine house in order: for thou shalt die, and not live. <hi type="super">2</hi> Then Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall, and prayed unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="super">3</hi> And said, Remember now, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , I beseech thee, how I have walked before thee in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done <hi type="italic">that which is</hi> good in thy sight. And Hezekiah wept sore. <hi type="super">4</hi> Then came the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> to Isaiah, saying, <hi type="super">5</hi> Go, and say to Hezekiah, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the God of David thy father, I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears: behold, I will add unto thy days fifteen years. <hi type="super">6</hi> And I will deliver thee and this city out of the hand of the king of Assyria: and I will defend this city. <hi type="super">7</hi> And this <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a sign unto thee from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will do this thing that he hath spoken; <hi type="super">8</hi> Behold, I will bring again the shadow of the degrees, which is gone down in the sun dial of Ahaz, ten degrees backward. So the sun returned ten degrees, by which degrees it was gone down. <div eID="gen16281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16282" type="x-p"/> We may hence observe, among others, these good lessons:—1. That neither men's greatness nor their goodness will exempt them from the arrests of sickness and death. Hezekiah, a mighty potentate on earth and a mighty favourite of Heaven, is struck with a disease, which, without a miracle, will certainly be mortal; and this in the midst of his days, his comforts, and usefulness. <hi type="italic">Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick.</hi> It should seem, this sickness seized him when he was in the midst of his triumphs over the ruined army of the Assyrians, to teach us always to rejoice with trembling. 2. It concerns us to prepare when we see death approaching: "<hi type="italic">Set thy house in order,</hi> and thy heart especially; put both thy affections and thy affairs into the best posture thou canst, that, when thy Lord comes, thou mayest be found of him in peace with God, with thy own conscience, and with all men, and mayest have nothing else to do but to die." Our being ready for death will make it come never the sooner, but much the easier: and those that are fit to die are most fit to live. 3. Is any afflicted with sickness? <hi type="italic">Let him pray,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.5.13">James v. 13</reference>. Prayer is a salve for every sore, personal or public. When Hezekiah was distressed by his enemies he prayed; now that he was sick he prayed. Whither should the child go, when any thing ails him, but to his Father? Afflictions are sent to bring us to our Bibles and to our knees. When Hezekiah was in health he <hi type="italic">went up to the house of the Lord</hi> to pray, for that was then the house of prayer. When he was sick in bed <hi type="italic">he turned his face towards the wall,</hi> probably towards the temple, which was a type of Christ, to whom we must look by faith in every prayer. 4. The testimony of our consciences for us that by the grace of God we have lived a good life, and have walked closely and humbly with God, will be a great support and comfort to us when we come to look death in the face. And though we may not depend upon it as our righteousness, by which to be justified before God, yet we may humbly plead it as an evidence of our interest in the righteousness of the Mediator. Hezekiah does not demand a reward from God for his good services, but modestly begs that God would remembers, not how he had reformed the kingdom, taken away the high places, cleansed the temple, and revived neglected ordinances, but, which was <hi type="italic">better than all burnt-offerings and sacrifices,</hi> how he had approved himself to God with a single eye and an honest heart, not only in these eminent performances, but in an even regular course of holy living: <hi type="italic">I have walked before thee in truth</hi> and sincerity, <hi type="italic">and with a perfect,</hi> that is, an upright, <hi type="italic">heart;</hi> for uprightness is our gospel perfection. 5. God has a gracious ear open to the prayers of his afflicted people. The same prophet that was sent to Hezekiah with warning to prepare for death is sent to him with a promise that he shall not only recover, but be restored to a confirmed state of health and live fifteen years yet. As Jerusalem was distressed, so Hezekiah was diseased, that God might have the glory of the deliverance of both, and that prayer too might have the honour of being instrumental in the deliverance. When we pray in our sickness, though God send not to us such an answer as he here sent to Hezekiah, yet, if by his Spirit he bids us be of good cheer, assures us that our sins are forgiven us, that his grace shall be sufficient for us, and that, whether we live or die, we shall be his, we have no reason to say that we pray in vain. God answers us if he <hi type="italic">strengthens us with strength in our souls,</hi> though not with bodily strength, <reference osisRef="Ps.138.3">Ps. cxxxviii. 3</reference>. 6. A good man cannot take much comfort in his own health and prosperity unless withal he see the welfare and prosperity of the church of God. Therefore God, knowing what lay near Hezekiah's heart, promised him not only that he should live, but that he should <hi type="italic">see the good of Jerusalem all the days of his life</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.128.5">Ps. cxxviii. 5</reference>), otherwise he cannot live comfortably. Jerusalem, which is now delivered, shall still be defended from the Assyrians, who perhaps threatened to rally again and renew the attack. Thus does God graciously provide to make Hezekiah upon all accounts easy. 7. God is <hi type="italic">willing to show to the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel,</hi> that they may have an unshaken faith in it, and therewith a strong consolation. God had given Hezekiah repeated assurances of his favour; and yet, as if all were thought too little, that he might expect from him uncommon favours, a sign is given him, an uncommon sign. None that we know of having had an absolute promise of living a certain number of years to come, as Hezekiah had, God thought fit to confirm this unprecedented favour with a miracle. The sign was the going back of the shadow upon the sun-dial. The sun is a faithful measurer of time, and <hi type="italic">rejoices as a strong man to run a race;</hi> but he that set that clock a going can set it back when he pleases, and make it to return; for the Father of all lights is the director of them.
entries.855a8d1349e82346bfb92b75d8e356a8c3405e3a: <div eID="gen16282" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Hezekiah's Thanksgiving. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen16283" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> The writing of Hezekiah king of Judah, when he had been sick, and was recovered of his sickness: <hi type="super">10</hi> I said in the cutting off of my days, I shall go to the gates of the grave: I am deprived of the residue of my years. <hi type="super">11</hi> I said, I shall not see the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">even</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , in the land of the living: I shall behold man no more with the inhabitants of the world. <hi type="super">12</hi> Mine age is departed, and is removed from me as a shepherd's tent: I have cut off like a weaver my life: he will cut me off with pining sickness: from day <hi type="italic">even</hi> to night wilt thou make an end of me. <hi type="super">13</hi> I reckoned till morning, <hi type="italic">that,</hi> as a lion, so will he break all my bones: from day <hi type="italic">even</hi> to night wilt thou make an end of me. <hi type="super">14</hi> Like a crane <hi type="italic">or</hi> a swallow, so did I chatter: I did mourn as a dove: mine eyes fail <hi type="italic">with looking</hi> upward: <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , I am oppressed; undertake for me. <hi type="super">15</hi> What shall I say? he hath both spoken unto me, and himself hath done <hi type="italic">it:</hi> I shall go softly all my years in the bitterness of my soul. <hi type="super">16</hi> O Lord, by these <hi type="italic">things men</hi> live, and in all these <hi type="italic">things is</hi> the life of my spirit: so wilt thou recover me, and make me to live. <hi type="super">17</hi> Behold, for peace I had great bitterness: but thou hast in love to my soul <hi type="italic">delivered it</hi> from the pit of corruption: for thou hast cast all my sins behind thy back. <hi type="super">18</hi> For the grave cannot praise thee, death can <hi type="italic">not</hi> celebrate thee: they that go down into the pit cannot hope for thy truth. <hi type="super">19</hi> The living, the living, he shall praise thee, as I <hi type="italic">do</hi> this day: the father to the children shall make known thy truth. <hi type="super">20</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">was ready</hi> to save me: therefore we will sing my songs to the stringed instruments all the days of our life in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">21</hi> For Isaiah had said, Let them take a lump of figs, and lay <hi type="italic">it</hi> for a plaster upon the boil, and he shall recover. <hi type="super">22</hi> Hezekiah also had said, What <hi type="italic">is</hi> the sign that I shall go up to the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ? <div eID="gen16283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16284" type="x-p"/> We have here Hezekiah's thanksgiving-song, which he penned, by divine direction, after his recovery. He might have taken some of the psalms of his father David, and made use of them for his purpose; he might have found many very pertinent ones. He appointed <hi type="italic">the Levites to praise the Lord with the words of David,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.29.30">2 Chron. xxix. 30</reference>. But the occasion here was extraordinary, and, his heart being full of devout affections, he would not confine himself to the compositions he had, though of divine inspiration, but would offer up his affections in his own words, which is most natural and genuine. He put this thanksgiving in writing, that he might review it himself afterwards, for the reviving of the good impressions made upon him by the providence, and that it might be recommended to others also for their use upon the like occasion. Note, There are writings which it is proper for us to draw up after we have been sick and have recovered. It is good to write a memorial of the affliction, and of the frame of our hearts under it,—to keep a record of the thoughts we had of things when we were sick, the affections that were then working in us,—to write a memorial of the mercies of a sick bed, and of our release from it, that they may never be forgotten,—to write a thanksgiving to God, write a sure covenant with him, and seal it,—to give it under our hands that we will never return again to folly. It is an excellent writing which Hezekiah here left, upon his recovery; and yet we find (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.25">2 Chron. xxxii. 25</reference>) that <hi type="italic">he rendered not again according to the benefit done to him.</hi> The impressions, one would think, should never have worn off, and yet, it seems, they did. Thanksgiving is good, but thanksliving is better. Now in this writing he preserves upon record, <div eID="gen16284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16285" type="x-p"/> I. The deplorable condition he was in when his disease prevailed, and his despair of recovery, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.10-Isa.38.13">v. 10-13</reference>. <div eID="gen16285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16286" type="x-p"/> 1. He tells us what his thoughts were of himself when he was at the worst; and these he keeps in remembrance, (1.) As blaming himself for his despondency, and that he gave up himself for gone; whereas while there is life there is hope, and room for our prayer and God's mercy. Though it is good to consider sickness as a summons to the grave, so as thereby to be quickened in our preparations for another world, yet we ought not to make the worse of our case, nor to think that every sick man must needs be a dead man presently. He that brings low can raise up. Or, (2.) As reminding himself of the apprehensions he had of death approaching, that he might always know and consider his own frailty and mortality, and that, though he had a reprieve for fifteen years, it was but a reprieve, and the fatal stroke he had now such a dread of would certainly come at last. Or, (3.) As magnifying the power of God in restoring him when his case was desperate, and his goodness in being so much better to him than his own fears. Thus David sometimes, when he was delivered out of trouble, reflected upon the black and melancholy conclusions he had made upon his own case when he was in trouble, and what he had then <hi type="italic">said in his haste,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Ps.31.22">Ps. xxxi. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.77.7-Ps.77.9">lxxvii. 7-9</reference>. <div eID="gen16286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16287" type="x-p"/> 2. Let us see what Hezekiah's thoughts of himself were. <div eID="gen16287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16288" type="x-p"/> (1.) He reckoned that the number of his months was cut off in the midst. He was now about thirty-nine or forty years of age, and when he had a fair prospect of many years and happy ones, very happy, very many, before him. This distemper that suddenly seized him he concluded would be the <hi type="italic">cutting off of his days,</hi> that he should now be <hi type="italic">deprived of the residue of his years,</hi> which in a course of nature he might have lived (not which he could command as a debt due to him, but which he had reason to expect, considering the strength of his constitution), and with them he should be deprived not only of the comforts of life, but of all the opportunities he had of serving God and his generation. To the same purport (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.12">v. 12</reference>), "<hi type="italic">My age has departed</hi> and gone, and is removed from me as a shepherd's tent, out of which I am forcibly dislodged by the pulling of it down in an instant." Our present residence is but like that of a shepherd in his tent, a poor, mean, and cold lodging, where we are upon duty, and with a trust committed to our charge, as the shepherd has, of which we must give an account, and which will easily be taken down by the drawing of one pin or two. But observe, It is not the final period of our age, but only the removal of it to another world, where the tents of Kedar that are taken down, coarse, black, and weather-beaten, shall be set up again in the New Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">comely as the curtains of Solomon.</hi> He adds another similitude: <hi type="italic">I have cut off, like a weaver, my life.</hi> Not that he did by any act of his own cut off the thread of his life; but, being told that he must needs die, he was forced to cut off all his designs and projects, his <hi type="italic">purposes were broken off,</hi> even the <hi type="italic">thoughts of his heart,</hi> as Job's were, <reference osisRef="Job.17.11">ch. xvii. 11</reference>. Our days are compared to the weaver's shuttle (<reference osisRef="Job.7.6">Job vii. 6</reference>), passing and repassing very swiftly, every throw leaving a thread behind it; and, when they are finished, the thread is cut off, and the piece taken out of the loom, and shown to our Master, to be judged of whether it be well woven or no, that we may <hi type="italic">receive according to the things done in the body.</hi> But as the weaver, when he has cut off his thread, has done his work, and the toil is over, so a good man, when his life is cut off, his cares and fatigues are cut off with it, and he rests from his labours. "But did I say, <hi type="italic">I have cut off my life?</hi> No, my times are not in my own hand; they are in God's hand, and it is he that <hi type="italic">will cut me off from the thrum</hi> (so the margin reads it); he has appointed what shall be the length of the piece, and, when it comes to that length, he will cut it off." <div eID="gen16288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16289" type="x-p"/> (2.) He reckoned that he should go to the gates of the grave—to the grave, the gates of which are always open; for it is still crying, <hi type="italic">Give, give.</hi> The grave is here put not only for the sepulchre of his fathers, in which his body would be deposited with a great deal of pomp and magnificence (for he was buried in the chief of the sepulchres of the kings, and all <hi type="italic">Judah did him honour at his death,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.33">2 Chron. xxxii. 33</reference>), which yet he himself took no care of, nor gave any order about, when he was sick; but for the state of the dead, that is, the <hi type="italic">sheol,</hi> the <hi type="italic">hades,</hi> the invisible world, to which he saw his soul going. <div eID="gen16289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16290" type="x-p"/> (3.) He reckoned that he was deprived of all the opportunities he might have had of worshipping God and doing good in the world (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.1">v. 1</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I said,</hi>" [1.] "<hi type="italic">I shall not see the Lord,</hi> as he manifests himself in his temple, in his oracles and ordinances, <hi type="italic">even the Lord</hi> here <hi type="italic">in the land of the living.</hi>" He hopes to see him on the other side death, but he despairs of seeing him any more on this side death, as he had seen him in the sanctuary, <reference osisRef="Ps.63.2">Ps. lxiii. 2</reference>. He shall no more see (that is, serve) the Lord in the land of the living, the land of conflict between his kingdom and the kingdom of Satan, this seat of war. He dwells much upon this: <hi type="italic">I shall no more see the Lord, even the Lord;</hi> for a good man wishes not to live for any other end than that he may serve God and have communion with him. [2.] "<hi type="italic">I shall see man no more.</hi>" He shall see his subjects no more, whom he may protect and administer justice to, shall see no more objects of charity, whom he may relieve, shall see his friends no more, who were often sharpened by his countenance, as iron is by iron. Death puts an end to conversation, and removes our acquaintance into darkness, <reference osisRef="Ps.88.18">Ps. lxxxviii. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen16290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16291" type="x-p"/> (4.) He reckoned that the agonies of death would be very sharp and severe: "<hi type="italic">He will cut me off with pining sickness,</hi> which will waste me, and wear me off, quickly." The distemper increased so fast, without intermission or remission, either day or night, morning or evening, that he concluded it would soon come to a crisis and make an end of him—that God, whose servants all diseases are, would by them, <hi type="italic">as a lion, break all his bones</hi> with grinding pain, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.13">v. 13</reference>. He thought that next morning was the utmost he could expect to live in such pain and misery; when he had outlived the first day's illness the second day he repeated his fears, and concluded that this must needs be his last night: <hi type="italic">from day even to night wilt thou make an end of me.</hi> When we are sick we are very apt to be thus calculating our time, and, after all, we are still at uncertainty. It should be more our care how we shall get safely to another world than how long we are likely to live in this world. <div eID="gen16291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16292" type="x-p"/> II. The complaints he made in this condition (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.14">v. 14</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Like a crane, or swallow, so did I chatter;</hi> I made a noise as those birds do when they are frightened." See what a change sickness makes in a little time; he that, but the other day, spoke with so much freedom and majesty, nor, through the extremity of pain or deficiency of spirits, <hi type="italic">chatters like a crane or a swallow.</hi> Some think he refers to his praying in his affliction; it was so broken and interrupted with groanings which could not be uttered that it was more like the chattering of a crane or a swallow than what it used to be. Such mean thoughts had he of his own prayers, which yet were acceptable to God, and successful. He <hi type="italic">mourned like a dove,</hi> sadly, but silently and patiently. He had found God so ready to answer his prayers at other times that he could not but look upwards, in expectation of some relief now, but in vain: his <hi type="italic">eyes failed,</hi> and he saw no hopeful symptom, nor felt any abatement of his distemper; and therefore he prays, "<hi type="italic">I am oppressed,</hi> quite overpowered and ready to sink; <hi type="italic">Lord, undertake for me;</hi> bail me out of the hands of the serjeant that has arrested me; <hi type="italic">be surety for thy servant for good,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.119.122">Ps. cxix. 122</reference>. Come between me and the gates of the grave, to which I am ready to be hurried." When we recover from sickness, the divine pity does, as it were, beg a day for us, and undertakes we shall be forthcoming another time and answer the debt in full. And, when we receive the sentence of death within ourselves, we are undone if the divine grace do not undertake for us to carry us through the valley of the shadow of death, and to preserve us blameless to the heavenly kingdom on the other side of it—if Christ do not undertake for us, to bring us off in judgment, and present us to his Father, and to do all that for us which we need, and cannot do for ourselves. <hi type="italic">I am oppressed, ease me</hi> (so some read it); for, when we are agitated by a sense of guilt and the fear of wrath, nothing will make us easy but Christ's undertaking for us. <div eID="gen16292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16293" type="x-p"/> III. The grateful acknowledgment he makes of God's goodness to him in his recovery. He begins this part of the writing as one at a stand how to express himself (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.15">v. 15</reference>): "<hi type="italic">What shall I say?</hi> Why should I say so much by way of complaint when this is enough to silence all my complaints—<hi type="italic">He has spoken unto me;</hi> he has sent his prophet to tell me that I shall recover and live fifteen years yet; <hi type="italic">and he himself has done it:</hi> it is as sure to be done as if it were done already. What God has spoken he will himself do, for no word of his shall fall to the ground." God having spoken it, he is sure of it (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.16">v. 16</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou wilt restore me, and make me to live;</hi> not only restore me from this illness, but make me to live through the years assigned me." And, having this hope, <div eID="gen16293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16294" type="x-p"/> 1. He promises himself always to retain the impressions of his affliction (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.15">v. 15</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will go softly all my years in the bitterness of my soul,</hi> as one in sorrow for my sinful distrusts and murmurings under my affliction, as one in care to make suitable returns for God's favour to me and to make it appear that I have got good by the providences I have been under. <hi type="italic">I will go softly,</hi> gravely and considerately, and with thought and deliberation, not as many, who, when they have recovered, live as carelessly and as much at large as ever." Or, "I will go pleasantly" (so some understand it); "when God has delivered me I will walk cheerfully with him in all holy conversation, as having tasted that he is gracious." Or, "I will go softly, even <hi type="italic">after the bitterness of my soul</hi>" (so it may be read); "when the trouble is over I will endeavour to retain the impression of it, and to have the same thoughts of things that I had then." <div eID="gen16294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16295" type="x-p"/> 2. He will encourage himself and others with the experiences he had had of the goodness of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.16">v. 16</reference>): "<hi type="italic">By these things</hi> which thou hast done for me <hi type="italic">they live,</hi> the kingdom lives" (for the life of such a king was the life of the kingdom); "all that hear of it shall live and be comforted; by the same power and goodness that have restored me all men have their souls held in life, and they ought to acknowledge it. <hi type="italic">In all these things is the life of my spirit,</hi> my spiritual life, that is supported and maintained by what God has done for the preservation of my natural life." The more we taste of the loving-kindness of God in every providence the more will our hearts be enlarged to love him and live to him, and that will be the life of our spirit. Thus our souls live, and they shall praise him. <div eID="gen16295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16296" type="x-p"/> 3. He magnifies the mercy of his recovery, on several accounts. <div eID="gen16296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16297" type="x-p"/> (1.) That he was raised up from great extremity (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold, for peace I had great bitterness.</hi> When, upon the defeat of Sennacherib, he expected nothing but an uninterrupted peace to himself and his government, he was suddenly seized with sickness, which embittered all his comforts to him, and went to such a height that it seemed to be the bitterness of death itself—<hi type="italic">bitterness, bitterness,</hi> nothing but gall and wormwood. This was his condition when God sent him seasonable relief. <div eID="gen16297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16298" type="x-p"/> (2.) That it came from the love of God, from love to his soul. Some are spared and reprieved in wrath, that they may be reserved for some greater judgment when they have filled up the measure of their iniquities; but temporal mercies are sweet indeed to us when we can taste the love of God in them. <hi type="italic">He delivered me because he delighted in me</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.19">Ps. xviii. 19</reference>); and the word here signifies a very affectionate love: <hi type="italic">Thou hast loved my soul from the pit of corruption;</hi> so it runs in the original. God's love is sufficient to bring a soul from the pit of corruption. This is applicable to our redemption by Christ; it was in love to our souls, our poor perishing souls, that he delivered them from the bottomless pit, snatched them as brands out of everlasting burnings. <hi type="italic">In his love and in his pity he redeemed us.</hi> And the preservation of our bodies, as well as the provision made for them, is doubly comfortable when it is in love to our souls—when God repairs the house because he has a kindness for the inhabitant. <div eID="gen16298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16299" type="x-p"/> (3.) That it was the effect of the pardon of sin: "<hi type="italic">For thou hast cast all my sins behind thy back,</hi> and thereby hast <hi type="italic">delivered my soul from the pit of corruption,</hi> in love to it." Note, [1.] When God pardons sin he casts it behind his back, as not designing to look upon it with an eye of justice and jealousy. He remembers it no more, to visit for it. The pardon does not make the sin not to have been, or not to have been sin, but not to be punished as it deserves. When we cast our sins behind our back, and take no care to repent of them, God sets them before his face, and is ready to reckon for them; but when we set them before our face in true repentance, as David did when his sin was ever before him, God casts them behind his back. [2.] When God pardons sins he pardons all, casts them all behind his back, though they have been as scarlet and crimson. [3.] The pardoning of the sin is the delivering of the soul from the pit of corruption. [4.] It is pleasant indeed to think of our recoveries from sickness when we see them flowing from the remission of sin; then the cause is removed, and then it is in love to the soul. <div eID="gen16299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16300" type="x-p"/> (4.) That it was the lengthening out of his opportunity to glorify God in this world, which he made the business, and pleasure, and end of life. [1.] If this sickness had been his death, it would have put a period to that course of service for the glory of God and the good of the church which he was now pursuing, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.18">v. 18</reference>. Heaven indeed praises God, and the souls of the faithful, when at death they remove thither, do that work of heaven as the angels, and with the angels, there; but what is this world the better for that? What does that contribute to the support and advancement of God's kingdom among men in this state of struggle? <hi type="italic">The grave cannot praise God,</hi> nor the dead bodies that lie there. <hi type="italic">Death cannot celebrate him,</hi> cannot proclaim his perfections and favours, to invite others into his service. <hi type="italic">Those who go down to the pit,</hi> being no longer in a state of probation, nor living by faith in his promises, cannot give him honour by hoping for his truth. Those that lie rotting in the grave, as they are not capable of receiving any further mercy from God, so neither are they capable of offering any more praises to him, till they shall be raised at the last day, and then they shall both receive and give glory. [2.] Having recovered from it, he resolves not only to proceed, but to abound, in praising and serving God (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">The living, the living, he shall praise thee.</hi> They may do it; they have an opportunity of praising God, and that is the main thing that makes life valuable and desirable to a good man. Hezekiah was <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> glad to live, not that he might continue to enjoy his royal dignity and the honour and pleasure of his late successes, but that he might continue to praise God. The living must praise God; they live in vain if they do not. Those that have been dying and yet are living, whose life is from the dead, are in a special manner obliged to praise God, as being most sensibly affected with his goodness. Hezekiah, for his part, having recovered from this sickness, will make it his business to praise God: "<hi type="italic">I do it this day;</hi> let others do it in like manner." Those that give good exhortations should set good examples, and do themselves what they expect from others. "For my part," says Hezekiah, "<hi type="italic">the Lord was ready to save me;</hi> he not only did save me, but he was ready to do it just then when I was in the greatest extremity; his help came in seasonably; he showed himself willing and forward to save me. <hi type="italic">The Lord was to save me,</hi> was at hand to do it, saved me a the first word; and therefore," <hi type="italic">First,</hi> "I will publish and proclaim his praises. I and my family, I and my friends, I and my people, will have a concert of praise to his glory: <hi type="italic">We will sing my songs to the stringed instruments,</hi> that others may attend to them, and be affected with them, when they are in the most devout and serious frame in the house of the Lord." It is for the honour of God, and the edification of his church, that special mercies should be acknowledged in public praises, especially mercies to public persons, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.18-Ps.116.19">Ps. cxvi. 18, 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> "I will proceed and persevere in his praises." We should do so all the days of our life, because every day of our life is itself a fresh mercy and brings many fresh mercies along with it; and, as renewed mercies call for renewed praises, so former eminent mercies call for repeated praises. It is by the mercy of God that we live, and therefore, as long as we live, we must continue to praise him, while we have breath, nay, while we have being. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> "I will propagate and perpetuate his praises." We should not only praise him all the days of our life, but <hi type="italic">the father to the children should make known his truth,</hi> that the ages to come may give God the glory of his truth by trusting to it. It is the duty of parents to possess their children with a confidence in the truth of God, which will go far towards keeping them close to the ways of God. Hezekiah, doubtless, did this himself, and yet Manasseh his son walked not in his steps. Parents may give their children many good things, good instructions, good examples, good books, but they cannot give them grace. <div eID="gen16300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16301" type="x-p"/> IV. In the <reference osisRef="Isa.38.21-Isa.38.22">last two verses</reference> of this chapter we have two passages relating to this story which were omitted in the narrative of it here, but which we had <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.1-2Kgs.20.21">2 Kings xx.</reference>, and therefore shall here only observe two lessons from them:—1. That God's promises are intended not to supersede, but to quicken and encourage, the use of means. Hezekiah is sure to recover, and yet he must <hi type="italic">take a lump of figs and lay it on the boil,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.38.21">v. 21</reference>. We do not trust God, but tempt him, if, when we pray to him for help, we do not second our prayers with our endeavours. We must not put physicians, or physic, in the place of God, but make use of them in subordination to God and to his providence; help thyself and God will help thee. 2. That the chief end we should aim at, in desiring life and health, is that we may glorify God, and do good, and improve ourselves in knowledge, and grace, and meetness for heaven. Hezekiah, when he meant, <hi type="italic">What is the sign that I shall recover?</hi> asked, <hi type="italic">What is the sign that I shall go up to the house of the Lord,</hi> there to honour God, to keep up acquaintance and communion with him, and to encourage others to serve him? <reference osisRef="Isa.38.22">v. 22</reference>. It is taken for granted that if God would restore him to health he would immediately go up to the temple with his thank-offerings. There Christ found the impotent man whom he had healed, <reference osisRef="John.5.14">John v. 14</reference>. The exercises of religion are so much the business and delight of a good man that to be restrained from them is the greatest grievance of his afflictions, and to be restored to them is the greatest comfort of his deliverances. <hi type="italic">Let my soul live, and it shall praise thee.</hi>  <chapter eID="Isa.38"/> <div eID="gen16301" type="x-p"/>

entries.e7fde1524b0b7618541a3e02a3510a4e5e4008df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9020"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 38</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.38.1-Isa.38.22">Is 38:1-22</reference>. Hezekiah's Sickness; Perhaps Connected with the Plague or Blast Whereby the Assyrian Army Had Been Destroyed.</title> <div sID="gen15181" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9020"/><hi type="bold">1. Set ... house in order--</hi>Make arrangement as to the succession to the throne; for he had then no son; and as to thy other concerns.<div eID="gen15181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15182" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou shall die--</hi>speaking according to the ordinary course of the disease. His being spared fifteen years was not a change in God's mind, but an illustration of God's dealings being unchangeably regulated by the state of man in relation to Him. <div eID="gen15182" type="x-p"/>
entries.04ed7f3a50429ab0ac63807d12d41c3c80488e5a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9021"/><div sID="gen15183" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9021"/>2. The couches in the East run along the walls of houses. He turned away from the spectators to hide his emotion and collect his thoughts for prayer. <div eID="gen15183" type="x-p"/>
entries.d00fe9157dec5e81039568076585fe6975485e23: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9022"/><div sID="gen15184" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9022"/>3. He mentions his past religious consistency, not as a boast or a ground for justification; but according to the Old Testament dispensation, wherein temporal rewards (as long life, &c., <reference osisRef="Exod.20.12">Ex 20:12</reference>) followed legal obedience, he makes his religious conduct a plea for asking the prolongation of his life.<div eID="gen15184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15185" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">walked--</hi>Life is a journey; the pious "walk with God" (<reference osisRef="Gen.5.24">Ge 5:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.4">1Ki 9:4</reference>).<div eID="gen15185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15186" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">perfect--</hi>sincere; not absolutely perfect, but aiming towards it (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.45">Mt 5:45</reference>); single-minded in walking as in the presence of God (<reference osisRef="Gen.17.1">Ge 17:1</reference>). The letter of the Old Testament legal righteousness was, however, a standard very much below the spirit of the law as unfolded by Christ (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.20-Matt.5.48">Mt 5:20-48</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.6">2Co 3:6</reference>, 14, 17).<div eID="gen15186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15187" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wept sore--</hi>Josephus says, the reason why he wept so sorely was that being childless, he was leaving the kingdom without a successor. How often our wishes, when gratified, prove curses! Hezekiah lived to have a son; that son was the idolater Manasseh, the chief cause of God's wrath against Judah, and of the overthrow of the kingdom (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.26">2Ki 23:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.27">27</reference>). <div eID="gen15187" type="x-p"/>
entries.2a3bd0278d97cba91843a55c721d69e71d99a94c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9023"/><div sID="gen15188" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9023"/>4. In <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.4">2Ki 20:4</reference>, the quickness of God's answer to the prayer is marked, "afore Isaiah had gone out into the middle court, the word of the Lord came to him"; that is, before he had left Hezekiah, or at least when he had just left him, and Hezekiah was in the act of praying after having heard God's message by Isaiah (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.65.24">Is 65:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.32.5">Psa 32:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.21">Da 9:21</reference>). <div eID="gen15188" type="x-p"/>
entries.a04338fdad28b66254240bd2874edb0eb9e73492: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9024"/><div sID="gen15189" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9024"/><hi type="bold">5. God of David thy father--</hi>God remembers the covenant with the father to the children (<reference osisRef="Exod.20.5">Ex 20:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.28">Psa 89:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.29">29</reference>).<div eID="gen15189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15190" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tears--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.56.8">Psa 56:8</reference>).<div eID="gen15190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15191" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">days ... years--</hi>Man's years, however many, are but as so many days (<reference osisRef="Gen.5.27">Ge 5:27</reference>). <div eID="gen15191" type="x-p"/>
entries.4d88e921bd5fc87567ca840c89a89f98e6e81d2f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9025"/><div sID="gen15192" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9025"/>6. In <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.8">2Ki 20:8</reference>, after this verse comes the statement which is put at the end, in order not to interrupt God's message (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.21">Is 38:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.22">22</reference>) by Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.5-Isa.38.8">Is 38:5-8</reference>).<div eID="gen15192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15193" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">will deliver--</hi>The city was already delivered, but here assurance is given, that Hezekiah shall have no more to fear from the Assyrians. <div eID="gen15193" type="x-p"/>
entries.67231a3d282087adab99120d356b60f2c2d80ff7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9026"/><div sID="gen15194" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9026"/><hi type="bold">7. sign--</hi>a token that God would fulfil His promise that Hezekiah should "go up into the house of the Lord the third day" (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.5">2Ki 20:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.8">8</reference>); the words in italics are not in Isaiah. <div eID="gen15194" type="x-p"/>
entries.c32d00d1dd8317921c5cf9b41281b5364209cbcf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9027"/><div sID="gen15195" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9027"/><hi type="bold">8. bring again--</hi>cause to return (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.12-Josh.10.14">Jos 10:12-14</reference>). In <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.9">2Ki 20:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.11">11</reference>, the choice is stated to have been given to Hezekiah, whether the shadow should go forward, or go back, ten degrees. Hezekiah replied, "It is a light thing (a less decisive miracle) for the shadow to go down (its usual direction) ten degrees: nay, but let it return backward ten degrees"; so Isaiah cried to Jehovah that it should be so, and it was so (compare <reference osisRef="Josh.10.12">Jos 10:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.14">14</reference>).<div eID="gen15195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15196" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sundial of Ahaz--</hi>Herodotus (2.109) states that the sundial and the division of the day into twelve hours, were invented by the Babylonians; from them Ahaz borrowed the invention. He was one, from his connection with Tiglath-pileser, likely to have done so (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.7">2Ki 16:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.10">10</reference>). "Shadow of the degrees" means the shadow made on the degrees. Josephus thinks these degrees were steps ascending to the palace of Ahaz; the time of day was indicated by the number of steps reached by the shadow. But probably a sundial, strictly so called, is meant; it was of such a size, and so placed, that Hezekiah, when convalescent, could witness the miracle from his chamber. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.38.21">Is 38:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.22">22</reference> with <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.9">2Ki 20:9</reference>, where translate, shall this shadow go forward, &c.; the dial was no doubt in sight, probably "in the middle court" (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.4">2Ki 20:4</reference>), the point where Isaiah turned back to announce God's gracious answers to Hezekiah. Hence this particular sign was given. The retrogression of the shadow may have been effected by refraction; a cloud denser than the air interposing between the gnomon and dial would cause the phenomenon, which does not take from the miracle, for God gave him the choice whether the shadow should go forward or back, and regulated the time and place. Bosanquet makes the fourteenth year of Hezekiah to be 689 B.C., the known year of a solar eclipse, to which he ascribes the recession of the shadow. At all events, there is no need for supposing any revolution of the relative positions of the sun and earth, but merely an effect produced on the shadow (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.9-2Kgs.20.11">2Ki 20:9-11</reference>); that effect was only local, and designed for the satisfaction of Hezekiah, for the Babylonian astronomers and king "sent to enquire of the wonder that was done in the land" (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.31">2Ch 32:31</reference>), implying that it had not extended to their country. No mention of any instrument for marking time occurs before this dial of Ahaz, 700 B.C. The first mention of the "hour" is made by Daniel at Babylon (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.6">Da 3:6</reference>). <div eID="gen15196" type="x-p"/>
entries.bcf2faecf16e468b3e2729a5ace564494db9e667: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9028"/><div sID="gen15197" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9028"/>9-20. The prayer and thanksgiving song of Hezekiah is only given here, not in the parallel passages of Second Kings and Second Chronicles. <reference osisRef="Isa.38.9">Is 38:9</reference> is the heading or inscription. <div eID="gen15197" type="x-p"/>
entries.a546bcf4da119a69296328a39d64c2c7a367efc4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9040"/><div sID="gen15237" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9040"/><hi type="bold">22. house of the Lord--</hi>Hence he makes the praises to be sung there prominent in his song (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.20">Is 38:20</reference>; Psa 116:12-14, 17-19). <chapter eID="Isa.38"/>

entries.be95a1e720e751b09c1518a4a08876bcd48a55d6: <div eID="gen28029" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen28030" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28031" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28031" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28030" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28032" type="x-p"/> Account of Hezekiah's dangerous sickness and miraculous recovery, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.1-Isa.38.9">Isa 38:1-9</reference>. Tender and beautiful song of thanksgiving, in which this pious king breathed out the sentiments of a grateful heart, when his life was, as it were, restored. This ode may be adapted to other cases; and will always afford profit and pleasure to those who are not void of feeling and piety, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.10-Isa.38.22">Isa 38:10-22</reference>. <div eID="gen28032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28033" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen28033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28034" type="x-p"/> In those days - The reader is requested to consult the notes on 2 Kings 20 in reference to the principal parts of this chapter.
entries.f2338490971c4537bd7c7fa801a1cc1f62b2c05a: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen28034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28035" type="x-p"/> Then Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall - The furniture of an eastern divan or chamber, either for the reception of company or for private use, consists chiefly of carpets spread on the floor in the middle; and of sofas, or couches ranged on one or more sides of the room, on a part raised somewhat above the floor. On these they repose themselves in the day, and sleep at night. It is to be observed that the corner of the room is the place of honor. Dr. Pococke, when he was introduced to the Sheikh of Furshout, found him sitting in the corner of his room. He describes another Arab Sheikh "as sitting in the corner of a large green tent, pitched in the middle of an encampment of Arabs; and the Bey of Girge as placed on a sofa in a corner to the right as one entered the room." - Harmer's Observ. 2 p. 60. Lady Mary Montague, giving an account of a visit which she made to the Kahya's lady at Adrianople, says, "She ordered cushions to be given me; and took care to place me in the corner, which is the place of honor." - Letter 33. The reason of this seems to be, that the person so placed is distinguished, and in a manner separated, from the rest of the company, and as it were guarded by the wall on each side. We are to suppose Hezekiah's couch placed in the same situation; in which turning on either side, he must turn his face to the wall; by which he would withdraw himself from those who were attending upon him in his apartment, in order to address his private prayer to God. <reference osisRef="Isa.38.3">Isa 38:3</reference> And he said, I beseech thee, O Jehovah, remember now how I have endeavored to walk before thee in truth, and with a perfect heart; and have done that which is good in thine eyes. And Hezekiah wept, and lamented grievously. - L. <reference osisRef="Isa.38.4">Isa 38:4</reference> Now [before Isaiah was gone out into the middle court] the word of Jehovah came unto him, saying, Go [back], and say unto Hezekiah, Thus saith Jehovah the God of David thy father, I have heard thy supplication; I have seen thy tears. Behold [I will heal thee; and on the third day thou shalt go up into the house of Jehovah. <reference osisRef="Isa.38.5">Isa 38:5</reference> And] I will add unto thy days fifteen years. And I will deliver thee, and this city, from the hand of the king of Assyria; and I will protect this city. And [Hezekiah said, By what sign shall I know that I shall go up into the house of Jehovah? <reference osisRef="Isa.38.7">Isa 38:7</reference> And Isaiah said], This shall be the sign unto thee from Jehovah, that Jehovah still bring to effect this word which he hath spoken. <div eID="gen28035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28036" type="x-p"/> The words in the translation included within crotchets are supplied from the parallel place, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.4">2Kgs 20:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.5">2Kgs 20:5</reference>, to make the narration more perfect. I have also taken the liberty, with Houbigant, of bringing forward the two last verses of this chapter, and inserting them in their proper places of the narration with the same mark. Kimchi's note on these two verses is as follows: "This and the following verse belong not to the writing of Hezekiah; and I see no reason why they are written here after the writing; for their right place is above, after And I will protect this city, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.6">Isa 38:6</reference>. And so they stand in the book of Kings, "<reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.7">2Kgs 20:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.8">2Kgs 20:8</reference>. The narration of this chapter seems to be in some parts an abridgment of that of 2 Kings 20. The abridger, having finished his extract here with the eleventh verse, seems to have observed, that the seventh and eighth verses of 2 Kings 20 were wanted to complete the narration: he therefore added them at the end of the chapter, after he had inserted the song of Hezekiah, probably with marks for their insertion in their proper places; which marks were afterwards neglected by transcribers. Or a transcriber might omit them by mistake, and add them at the end of the chapter with such marks. Many transpositions are, with great probability, to be accounted for in the same way.
entries.d67280ae69848610721056411b347b9947263dac: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen28036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28037" type="x-p"/> I will defend this city - The other copy, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.6">2Kgs 20:6</reference>, adds:" for mine own sake, and for the sake of David my servant;" and the sentence seems somewhat abrupt without it.
entries.c6ee0afe782f9915c94e565b2fc81f06eea06499: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen28037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28038" type="x-p"/> Which is gone down "By which the sun is gone down" - For בשמש bashshemesh, the Septuagint, Syriac, and Chaldee read השמש, hashshemesh. - Houbigant. In the history of this miracle in the book of Kings, (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.9-2Kgs.20.11">2Kgs 20:9-11</reference>), there is no mention at all made of the sun, but only of the going backward of the shadow: which might be effected by a supernatural refraction. The first ὁ ἡλιος, the sun, in this verse is omitted in the Septuagint, MS. Pachom.
entries.9a2a7df264cd8a3aab2f790adbc8f5df54f0e8dd: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen28038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28039" type="x-p"/> The writing of Hezekiah - Here the book of Kings deserts us, the song of Hezekiah not being inserted in it. Another copy of this very obscure passage (obscure not only from the concise poetical style, but because it is probably very incorrect) would have been of great service. <div eID="gen28039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28040" type="x-p"/> The MSS. and ancient Versions, especially the latter, will help us to get through some of the many difficulties which we meet with in it.
entries.a348bbdd577fa421a5213178411d5ca9c5a97d0e: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen28040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28041" type="x-p"/> The Lord "Jehovah" - יה Yah, יה Yah, seems to be יהוה Yehovah, in MS. Bodl., and it was so at first written in another. So the Syriac. See Houbigant. I believe יהוה Yehovah was the original reading. See the note on <reference osisRef="Isa.12.2">Isa 12:2</reference> (note).
entries.4cd5d4230f3b3ac974e6450be0537dbdebf834d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen28041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28042" type="x-p"/> Mine age - is removed from me as a shepherd's tent - רעי roi is put for רעה roeh, say the rabbis (Sal. Den Melec on the place); but much more probably is written imperfectly for רעים roim, shepherds. See note on <reference osisRef="Isa.5.1">Isa 5:1</reference>. <div eID="gen28042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28043" type="x-p"/> I shall be removed from this state to another, as a shepherd removes his tent from one place to another for the sake of his flock. Is not this a strong intimation of his belief in a future state? <div eID="gen28043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28044" type="x-p"/> I have cut off like a weaver my life "My life is cut off as by the weaver" - קפדתי kippadti. This verb is rendered passively, and in the third person, by the Syriac, Chaldee, and Vulgate.
entries.03cb73fe0c9e39bdd32c0408d5d02f9b8f6b7b01: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen28044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28045" type="x-p"/> The last line of the foregoing verse מיום עד לילה תשלימני miyom ad layelah tashlimeni, "In the course of the day thou wilt finish my web; "or, as the common version has it, "From day even to night wilt thou make an end of me, "is not repeated at the end of this verse in the Syriac version; and a MS. omits it. It seems to have been inserted a second time in the Hebrew text by mistake. <div eID="gen28045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28046" type="x-p"/> I reckoned till morning, etc. "I roared until the morning like the lion" - For שויתי shivvithi, the Chaldee has נהמית nihameith: he read שאגתי shaagti, the proper term for the roaring of a lion; often applied to the deep groaning of men in sickness. See Psalm 22, <reference osisRef="Psa.32.3">Psa 32:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.38.9">Psa 38:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.3.24">Job 3:24</reference>. The Masoretes divide the sentence, as I have done; taking כארי caari, like a lion, into the first member; and so likewise the Septuagint.
entries.126827b8bd2fec182dc2965a127b8251d93a93f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen28046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28047" type="x-p"/> Like - a swallow "Like the swallow" - כסיס kesis; so read two MSS., Theodot., and Hieron. <div eID="gen28047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28048" type="x-p"/> Mine eyes fail - For דלו dallu the Septuagint read כלו calu, εξελιπον. Compare <reference osisRef="Psa.69.4">Psa 69:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.119.82">Psa 119:82</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.119.123">Psa 119:123</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.11">Lam 2:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.4.17">Lam 4:17</reference>, in the Hebrew and in the Septuagint. <div eID="gen28048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28049" type="x-p"/> O Lord "O Lord" - For יהוה Jehovah, thirty MSS. and eight editions read אדני Adonai. <div eID="gen28049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28050" type="x-p"/> Undertake for me "Contend for me" - עשקה ashekah, with ש shin, Jarchi: this sense of the word is established by <reference osisRef="Gen.26.20">Gen 26:20</reference> : "He called the name of the well עשק esek, because they strove with him:" התעשקו hithasseku, equivalent to יריבו yaribu, at the beginning of the verse.
entries.e25b06af0455131f79d50b8205849bc885ab1abc: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen28050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28051" type="x-p"/> I shall go softly all my years in the bitterness of my soul "Through the rest of my years will I reflect on this bitterness of my soul" - אדדה eddaddeh; recogitabo, Vulg., reputabo, Hieron. in loc.
entries.68815e50dbb113be17e2ef784440ea5f0677488f: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen28051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28052" type="x-p"/> By these things men live "For this cause shall it be declared" - Περι αυτης γαρ ανηγγελη σοι, και εξηγειρας μου την πνοην, Sept. They read in their copies עליה יחוו לך ותחיי רוחי not very different from the present text, from which all the ancient Versions vary. They entirely omit two words, ולכל בהן ulecol bahen; as to which there is some variation in the MSS. One MS. has ובכל ubechol, and in all; two others וכל vechol, and all, and ten MSS. have בהם bahem, in them, in the masculine gender. <div eID="gen28052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28053" type="x-p"/> Taking this as in the common Version, we may observe, it is not an unfrequent case, that afflictions, and especially such as tend to a speedy death, become the means, not only of saving the soul, but also of lengthening the life. <div eID="gen28053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28054" type="x-p"/> Make me to live "Hast prolonged my life" - A MSS. and the Babylonish Talmud read ותחיני vetachayeni, and so the ancient Versions. It must necessarily be in the second person.
entries.ef1e98e023f141acc3be6aba9f34823b1b5128ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen28054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28055" type="x-p"/> For peace I had great bitterness "My anguish is changed into ease" - מר לי מר mar li mar, "mutata mthi est amaritudo." Paronomasia; a figure which the prophet frequently admits. I do not always note it, because it cannot ever be preserved in the translation, and the sense seldom depends upon it. But here it perfectly clears up the great obscurity of the passage. See Lowth on the place. <div eID="gen28055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28056" type="x-p"/> Thou hast rescued - חשכת chashachta, with כ caph, instead of ק koph; so the Septuagint and Vulgate; Houbigant. See Chappelow on <reference osisRef="Job.33.18">Job 33:18</reference>. <div eID="gen28056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28057" type="x-p"/> From perdition - משחת בלי mishshachath beli, ἱνα μη αποληται, Sept. ut non periret, "that it may not perish." Vulg. Perhaps inverting the order of the words. See Houbigant. <div eID="gen28057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28058" type="x-p"/> Thou hast in love to my soul - חשקת chashakta, "thou hast lovingly embraced" or kissed "my soul out of the pit of corruption."
entries.5e3c2fdfef8ec587a3a3d08938a02648f5156dcb: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen28058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28059" type="x-p"/> Thy truth - אל אמתך el amittecha. A MS. omits אל el; and instead of אל el, an ancient MS. and one edition read את eth. The same mistake as in <reference osisRef="Psa.2.7">Psa 2:7</reference>.
entries.c670bc89698e064fc782f219e18e9e7270a61ab3: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen28059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28060" type="x-p"/> Let them take a lump of figs, etc. - God, in effecting this miraculous cure, was pleased to order the use of means not improper for that end. "Folia, et, quae non maturuere, fici, strumis illinuntur omnibusque quae emollienda sunt discutiendave." - Plin. Nat. Hist. 23:7. "Ad discutienda ea, quae in corporis parte aliqua coierunt, maxime possunt-ficus arida," etc. - Celsus, 5:11. <div eID="gen28060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28061" type="x-p"/> See the note on <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.7">2Kgs 20:7</reference> (note). Philemon Holland translates the passage as a medical man: "The milke or white juice that the figge tree yieldeth is of the same nature that vinegre: and therefore it will cruddle milke as well as rennet, or rendles. The right season of gathering this milkie substance is before that the figs be ripe upon the tree; and then it must be dried in the shadow: thus prepared, it is good to break impostumes, and keepe ulcer open."  <chapter eID="Isa.38"/> <div eID="gen28061" type="x-p"/>

entries.cead9da1f46435ea369e66e008be1e7861e663a0: <div sID="gen13285" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="38" osisID="Isa.38" sID="Isa.38"/> <chapter n="38" osisID="Isa.38" sID="Isa.38"/>
entries.309b00dac86c06f4520c63e6133483a7acb39e3d: <reference osisRef="Isa.38.1-Isa.38.3">Isa 38:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen13285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13286" type="x-p"/> There is nothing to surprise us in the fact that we are carried back to the time when Jerusalem was still threatened by the Assyrian, since the closing vv. of chapter 37 merely contain an anticipatory announcement, introduced for the purpose of completing the picture of the last Assyrian troubles, by adding the fulfilment of Isaiah’s prediction of their termination. It is within this period, and indeed in the year of the Assyrian invasion (<reference osisRef="Isa.36.1">Isa 36:1</reference>), since Hezekiah reigned twenty-nine years, and fifteen of these are promised here, that the event described by Isaiah falls - an event not merely of private interest, but one of importance in connection with the history of the nation also. <hi type="italic">“In those days Hizkiyahu became dangerously ill. And Isaiah son of Amoz, the prophet, came to him, and said to him, Thus saith Jehovah, Set thine house in order: for thou wilt die, and not recover. Then Hizkiyahu turned </hi>(K. om.)<hi type="italic">his face to the wall, and prayed to Jehovah, and said </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">saying</hi>)<hi type="italic">, O Jehovah, remember this, I pray, that I have walked before thee in truth, and with the whole heart, and have done what was good in Thine eyes! And Hizkiyahu wept with loud weeping.”</hi> “Give command to thy house” (ל, cf., אל,   <reference osisRef="2Sam.17.23">2Sa 17:23</reference>) is equivalent to, “Make known thy last will to thy family” (compare the rabbinical <hi type="italic">tsavvâ'âh</hi>, the last will and testament); for though <hi type="italic">tsivvâh</hi> is generally construed with the accusative of the person, it is also construed with <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> (e.g., <reference osisRef="Exod.1.22">Exo 1:22</reference>; cf., אל, <reference osisRef="Exod.16.34">Exo 16:34</reference>). חיה in such a connection as this signifies to revive or recover. The announcement of his death is unconditional and absolute. As Vitringa observes, “the condition was not expressed, because God would draw it from him as a voluntary act.” The sick man turned his face towards the wall (פּניו הסב, hence the usual fut. cons. ויּסּב as in 1Ki 21:4, 1Ki 21:8, 1Ki 21:14), to retire into himself and to God. The supplicatory אנּה (here, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.116.4">Psa 116:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.16">Psa 116:16</reference>, and in all six times, with ה) always has the principal tone upon the last syllable before יהוה = אדני (<reference osisRef="Neh.1.11">Neh 1:11</reference>). The <hi type="italic">metheg</hi> has sometimes passed into a conjunctive accent (e.g., <reference osisRef="Gen.50.17">Gen 50:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.32.31">Exo 32:31</reference>). אשׁר את does not signify that which, but this, that, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.9.7">Deu 9:7</reference>; 2Ki 8:12, etc. “In truth,” i.e., without wavering or hypocrisy. שׁלם בלב, with a complete or whole heart, as in 1Ki 8:61, etc. He wept aloud, because it was a dreadful thing to him to have to die without an heir to the throne, in the full strength of his manhood (in the thirty-ninth year of his age), and with the nation in so unsettled a state.
entries.ff0f970733fe5e840d950150208be56f05b20ae1: <reference osisRef="Isa.38.4-Isa.38.6">Isa 38:4-6</reference> <div eID="gen13286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13287" type="x-p"/> The prospect is now mercifully changed. <hi type="italic">“And it came to pass </hi>(K. <hi type="italic">Isaiah was not yet out of the inner city;</hi> keri סהצר,<hi type="italic">the forecourt, and</hi>)<hi type="italic">the word of Jehovah came to Isaiah </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">to him) as follows: Go </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">turn again) and say to Hizkiyahu </hi>(K. adds,<hi type="italic">to the prince of my people</hi>),<hi type="italic">Thus saith Jehovah, the God of David thine ancestor, I have heard thy prayer, seen thy tears; behold, I </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">will cure thee, on the third day thou shalt go up to the house of Jehovah</hi>)<hi type="italic">add </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">and I add) to thy days fifteen years. And I will deliver thee ad this city out of the hand of the king of Asshur, and will defend this city </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">for mine own sake and for David my servant’s sake</hi>)<hi type="italic">.”</hi> In the place of העיר (the city) the <hi type="italic">keri</hi> and the earlier translators have הצר. The city of David is not called the “inner city” anywhere else; in fact, Zion, with the temple hill, formed the upper city, so that apparently it is the inner space of the city of David that is here referred to, and Isaiah had not yet passed through the middle gate to return to the lower city, where he dwelt. The text of Kings is the more authentic throughout; except that עמּי נגיד, “the prince of my people,” is an annalistic adorning which is hardly original. סהלוך in Isaiah is an inf. abs. used in an imperative sense; שׁוּב, on the other hand, which we find in the other text, is imperative. On <hi type="italic">yōsiph</hi>, see at Isa 29:14.
entries.47b0f7dc7fee313f6448325973a0d844ca8f78ac: <reference osisRef="Isa.38.7-Isa.38.8">Isa 38:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen13287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13288" type="x-p"/> The pledge desired. <hi type="italic">“</hi>(K.<hi type="italic">Then Isaiah said</hi>)<hi type="italic">and </hi>(K. om.)<hi type="italic">let this be the sign to thee on the part of Jehovah, that </hi>(אשׁר, K. כּי)<hi type="italic">Jehovah will perform this</hi> (K.<hi type="italic">the</hi>)<hi type="italic">word which He has spoken; Behold, I make the shadow retrace the steps, which it has gone down upon the sun-dial of Ahaz through the sun, ten steps backward. And the sun went back ten steps upon the dial, which it had gone down” </hi>(K. <hi type="italic">“Shall the shadow go forward </hi>[הלך, read הלך according to <reference osisRef="Job.40.2">Job 40:2</reference>, or הילך]<hi type="italic">ten steps, or shall it go back ten steps? Then Yechizkiyahu said, It is easy for the shadow to go down ten steps; no, but the shadow shall go back ten steps. Then Isaiah the prophet cried to Jehovah, and turned back the shadow by the steps that it had gone down upon the sun-dial of Ahaz, ten steps backward”</hi>)<hi type="italic">. “Steps of Ahaz”</hi> was the name given to a sun-dial erected by him. As <hi type="italic">ma‛ălâh</hi> may signify either one of a flight of steps or a degree (syn. <hi type="italic">madrigâh</hi>), we might suppose the reference to be to a dial-plate with a gnomon; but, in the first place, the expression points to an actual succession of steps, that is to say, to an obelisk upon a square or circular elevation ascended by steps, which threw the shadow of its highest point at noon upon the highest steps, and in the morning and evening upon the lowest either on the one side or the other, so that the obelisk itself served as a gnomon. It is in this sense that the Targum on 2Ki 9:13 renders <hi type="italic">gerem</hi> <hi type="italic">hamma‛ălōth</hi> by <hi type="italic">derag</hi> <hi type="italic">shâ‛ayyâ'</hi>, step (flight of steps) of the sun-dial; and the obelisk of Augustus, on the Field of Mars at Rome, was one of this kind, which served as a sun-dial. The going forward, going down, or declining of the shadow, and its going back, were regulated by the meridian line, and under certain circumstances the same might be said of a vertical dial, i.e., of a sun-dial with a vertical dial-plate; but it applies more strictly to a step-dial, i.e., to a sun-dial in which the degrees that measure definite periods of time are really <hi type="italic">gradus</hi>. The step-dial of Ahaz may have consisted of twenty steps or more, which measured the time of day by half-hours, or even quarters. If the sign was given an hour before sunset, the shadow, by going back ten steps of half-an-hour each, would return to the point at which it stood at twelve o'clock. But how was this effected? Certainly not by giving an opposite direction to the revolution of the earth upon its axis, which would have been followed by the most terrible convulsions over the entire globe; and in all probability not even by an apparently retrograde motion of the sun (in which case the miracle would be optical rather than cosmical); but as the intention was to give a sign that should serve as a pledge, and therefore had not need whatever to be supernatural, it may have been simply through a phenomenon of refraction, since all that was required was that the shadow which was down at the bottom in the afternoon should be carried upwards by a sudden and unexpected refraction. <hi type="italic">Hamma‛ălōth</hi> (the steps) in <reference osisRef="Isa.38.8">Isa 38:8</reference> does not stand in a genitive relation to <hi type="italic">tsēl</hi> (the shadow), as the accents would make it appear, but is an accusative of measure, equivalent to בּמּעלות in the sum of the steps (2Ki 20:11). To this accusative of measure there is appended the relative clause: <hi type="italic">quos</hi> (<hi type="italic">gradus</hi>) <hi type="italic">descendit</hi> (ירדה; צל being used as a feminine) <hi type="italic">in scala Ahasi per solem</hi>, i.e., through the onward motion of the sun. When it is stated that “the sun returned,” this does not mean the sun in the heaven, but the sun upon the sun-dial, upon which the illuminated surface moved upwards as the shadow retreated; for when the shadow moved back, the sun moved back as well. The event is intended to be represented as a miracle; and a miracle it really was. The force of will proved itself to be a power superior to all natural law; the phenomenon followed upon the prophet’s prayer as an extraordinary result of divine power, not effected through his astronomical learning, but simply through that faith which can move mountains, because it can set in motion the omnipotence of God. <reference osisRef="Isa.38.7-Isa.38.8">Isa 38:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen13722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13723" type="x-p"/> On 2Ki 20:9 - Even הלך is syntactically admissible in the sense of <hi type="italic">iveritne</hi>; see <reference osisRef="Gen.21.7">Gen 21:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.11.3">Psa 11:3</reference>; Job 12:9. <reference osisRef="Isa.47.12-Isa.47.15">Isa 47:12-15</reference> ἀλμενιχακά in Plut., read Porph., viz., in the letter of Porphyrios to the Egyptian Anebo in Euseb. <hi type="italic">praep</hi>. iii. 4, <hi type="italic">init</hi>.: τάς τε εἰς τοὺς δεκανοὺς τομὰς καὶ τοὺς ὡροσκόποὺς καὶ τοὺς λεγομένους κραταιοὺς ἡγεμόνας, ὧν καὶ ὀνόματα ἐν τοῖς ἀλμενιχιακοῖς φέρεται; compare Jamblichos, <hi type="italic">de Mysteriis</hi>, viii. 4: τά τε ἑν τοῖς σαλμεσχινιακοῖς μέρος τι βραχύτατον περιέχει τῶν ̔Ερμαικῶν διατάξεων. This reading σαλμεσχινιακοῖς has been adopted by Parthey after two codices and the text in Salmasius, <hi type="italic">de annis clim</hi>. 605. But ἀλμενιχιακοῖς is favoured by the form <hi type="italic">Almanach</hi> (Hebr. אלמנק, see Steinschneider, <hi type="italic">Catal. Codd. Lugduno-Batav</hi>. p. 370), in which the word was afterwards adopted as the name of an astrological handbook or year-book. In Arabic the word appears to me to be equivalent to <hi type="italic">'l - mnâch</hi>, the <hi type="italic">encampment</hi> (of the stars); but to all appearance it was originally an Egyptian word, and possibly the Coptic <hi type="italic">monk</hi> (old Egyptian <hi type="italic">mench</hi>), a form or thing formed, is hidden beneath it. <reference osisRef="Isa.57.10">Isa 57:10</reference> נואשׁ - Fleischer says: “Just as in Arabic <hi type="italic">'ml</hi> and <hi type="italic">rj'</hi> the meaning of hope springs out of the idea of stretching and drawing out, so do Arabic <hi type="italic">ayisa</hi> and <hi type="italic">ya'isa</hi> (<hi type="italic">spem deposuit</hi>, <hi type="italic">desperavit</hi>) signify literally to draw in, to compress; hence the old Arabic <hi type="italic">ya'asun</hi> = <hi type="italic">sillun</hi>, consumption, <hi type="italic">phthisis</hi>. And the other old Arabic word <hi type="italic">waysun</hi>, lit., squeezing, <hi type="italic">res angustae</hi> = <hi type="italic">fakr wa-faka</hi>, want, need, and penury, or in a concrete sense the need, or thing needed, is also related to this.” <reference osisRef="Isa.65.11">Isa 65:11</reference> Μήνη appears in μηναγύρθς = μητραγύρθς as the name of Cybele, the mother of the gods. In Egyptian, <hi type="italic">Menhi</hi> is a form of Isis in the city of <hi type="italic">Hat-uer</hi>. The Ithyphallic <hi type="italic">Min</hi>, the cognomen of Amon, which is often written in an abbreviated form with the spelling <hi type="italic">men</hi> (Copt. <hi type="italic">MHIN</hi>, <hi type="italic">signum</hi>), is further removed.  <chapter eID="Isa.38"/> <div eID="gen13723" type="x-p"/>
entries.758ed3b66e51a8b8bbd1a56651fa9eb5bf68aa74: <reference osisRef="Isa.38.9">Isa 38:9</reference> <div eID="gen13288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13289" type="x-p"/> As a documentary proof of this third account, a psalm of Hezekiah is added in the text of Isaiah, in which he celebrates his miraculous rescue from the brink of death. The author of the book of Kings has omitted it; but the genuineness is undoubted. The heading runs thus in <reference osisRef="Isa.38.9">Isa 38:9</reference> : <hi type="italic">“Writing of Hizkiyahu king of Judah, when he was sick, and recovered from his sickness.”</hi> The song which follows might be headed <hi type="italic">Mikhtam</hi>, since it has the characteristics of this description of psalm (see at <reference osisRef="Ps.16.1">Psa 16:1</reference>). We cannot infer from <hi type="italic">bachălōthō</hi> (when he was sick) that it was composed by Hezekiah during his illness (see at <reference osisRef="Ps.51.1">Psa 51:1</reference>); <hi type="italic">vayyechi</hi> (and he recovered) stamps it as a song of thanksgiving, composed by him after his recovery. In common with the two Ezrahitish psalms, Ps 88 and 89, it has not only a considerable number of echoes of the book of Job, but also a lofty sweep, which is rather forced than lyrically direct, and appears to aim at copying the best models.
entries.cdac8638e1013ab7b160306423ab8422e13cc209: <reference osisRef="Isa.38.10-Isa.38.12">Isa 38:10-12</reference> <hi type="italic">Strophe</hi> 1 consists indisputably of seven lines:<hi type="italic">“I said, In quiet of my days shall I depart into the gates of Hades: I am mulcted of the rest of my years. I said, I shall not see Jah, Jah, in the land of the living: I shall behold man no more, with the inhabitants of the regions of the dead. My home is broken up, and is carried off from me like a shepherd’s tent: I rolled up my life like a weaver; He would have cut me loose from the roll: From day to night Thou makest an end of me.” </hi> “In quiet of my days” is equivalent to, in the midst of the quiet course of a healthy life, and is spoken without reference to the Assyrian troubles, which still continued. דּמי, from דּמה, to be quiet, lit., to be even, for the radical form דם has the primary idea of a flat covering, of something stroked smooth, of that which is level and equal, so that it could easily branch out into the different ideas of <hi type="italic">aequabilitas</hi>, equality of measure, <hi type="italic">aequitas</hi>, equanimity, <hi type="italic">aequitas</hi>, equality, and also of destruction = <hi type="italic">complanatio</hi>, levelling. On the cohortative, in the sense of that which is to be, see Ewald, §228, a; אלכה, according to its verbal idea, has the same meaning as in Ps. 39:14 and <reference osisRef="2Chr.21.20">2Ch 21:20</reference>; and the construction with בּ (= ואבואה אלכה) is <hi type="italic">constructio praegnans</hi> (Luzzatto). The <hi type="italic">pual</hi> פּקּדתּי does not mean, “I am made to want” (Rashi, Knobel, and others), which, as the passive of the causative, would rather be הפקשׂדתּי, like הנסהלתּי, I am made to inherit (<reference osisRef="Job.7.3">Job 7:3</reference>); but, I am visited with punishment as to the remnant, mulcted of the remainder, deprived, as a punishment, of the rest of my years. The clause, “Jah in the land of the living,” i.e., the God of salvation, who reveals Himself in the land of the living, is followed by the corresponding clause, הדל עם־יושׁבי, “I dwelling with the inhabitants of the region of the dead;” for whilst הלד signifies temporal life (from <hi type="italic">châlad</hi>, to glide imperceptibly away, <reference osisRef="Job.11.17">Job 11:17</reference>), הלד signifies the end of this life, the negation of all conscious activity of being, the region of the dead.
